ai.definition: A Quantum Gravity Probe is a hypothetical device designed to measure the minute effects of gravity on subatomic particles, aiming to explore the intersection between quantum mechanics and general relativity.
ai.howItWorks: The probe would integrate advanced quantum sensors with gravitational wave detectors. By observing how subatomic particles behave in extremely precise gravitational fields, it could provide insights into the unification of these two fundamental theories of physics.
ai.problemSolved: Addresses the theoretical gap between quantum mechanics and general relativity by directly measuring the effects of gravity at the quantum scale, potentially leading to a more unified theory of physics.
ai.manufacturing: Current technology is not mature enough for practical manufacturing; research is focused on developing the necessary precision in both quantum sensors and gravitational wave detectors.
ai.buildProcess: Involves complex theoretical modeling, experimental setup design, and precise fabrication techniques. Requires interdisciplinary collaboration between physicists specializing in quantum mechanics and gravitational physics.
ai.costDrivers: High due to the need for cutting-edge technology, specialized equipment, and extremely controlled experimental environments. Development costs are likely to be in the millions of dollars over several years.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Long-term potential with significant scientific breakthroughs if successful, but current stage is highly speculative and dependent on technological advancements.
ai.regulation: No specific regulatory framework exists for this technology as it is still in the conceptual phase. However, any practical application would likely require approval from relevant science funding bodies and safety regulations.
ai.risks: High technical risks due to the complexity of the required technologies. Financial risk due to potential long-term development periods without guaranteed returns.
ai.profitability: Uncertain; primarily a scientific endeavor aimed at advancing fundamental knowledge rather than direct commercial application in the near term.
ai.futureDevelopment: Potential for significant scientific breakthroughs, but requires substantial investment and collaboration across multiple scientific disciplines. Long-term implications could include new technologies based on advanced quantum sensors or gravitational wave detection.

glossary.def: A fundamental theory in physics that describes the physical properties of nature at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles.
A theory of gravitation developed by Albert Einstein, describing gravity as a curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy.
A mathematical model that combines three dimensions of space and one dimension of time into a single four-dimensional continuum.

subsystems.name: Quantum sensor
subsystems.role: the mass or atom wave whose phase shifts in a gravitational field.
parts: or a levitated microsphere in an optical trap

subsystems.name: Interferometer and readout
subsystems.role: turns tiny phase shifts into a measurable signal.

subsystems.name: Isolation and shielding
subsystems.role: keeps seismic, magnetic, thermal and acoustic noise from swamping the signal.

subsystems.name: Baseline structure
subsystems.role: separates the sensor elements by a known distance.
parts: long vacuum tube or free-fall drift

subsystems.name: Calibration and analysis
subsystems.role: distinguishes new physics from conventional disturbances.

buildSteps.title: Pick the observable
buildSteps.detail: Choose a signature that quantum-gravity theories actually predict at reachable energies — a deviation from Newtonian gravity at short range, a loss of quantum coherence, or entanglement between two masses caused only by their gravity.

buildSteps.title: Design the sensor
buildSteps.detail: Decide between atom interferometry (two atom clouds in free fall), levitated optomechanics (a nanoparticle held in a laser trap), or suspended masses. Each sets the required vacuum, laser and cryogenic budget.

buildSteps.title: Build the vacuum and baseline
buildSteps.detail: Make a long, straight, evacuated tube or a drop tower, held at pressure low enough that residual gas does not scatter the sensor.

buildSteps.title: Install the quantum optics
buildSteps.detail: Add lasers, optical cavities, atom sources and detectors, aligned to fractions of a wavelength over the whole baseline.

buildSteps.title: Isolate from the environment
buildSteps.detail: Mount on seismic isolation, shield magnetically and thermally, and characterise every residual vibration and gravity gradient.

buildSteps.title: Calibrate with known masses
buildSteps.detail: Move a measured mass and confirm the instrument recovers the expected Newtonian signal before claiming any anomaly.

buildSteps.title: Run and analyse
buildSteps.detail: Collect data for long periods, look for a signal that grows with mass and shrinks with distance in the predicted way, and test alternative explanations.

buildSteps.title: Replicate elsewhere
buildSteps.detail: Reproduce the result on an independent apparatus — the step that separates a discovery from an artefact.

prerequisites.why: provides the quantum sensors that respond to gravity over metre-scale baselines.
already used in gravitational-wave detectors to measure displacements below the standard quantum limit.
needed to hold a macroscopic-enough mass in a genuine quantum superposition long enough to see gravity act on it.

prerequisites.tech: Sensitivity to gravity over short baselines
prerequisites.why: probes so far reach distances far above any predicted quantum-gravity scale.
most quantum-gravity theories make no falsifiable prediction at energies any experiment can reach.

pathway.milestone: long-baseline atom interferometers under construction, for example the 100 m MAGIS-100 at Fermilab and the AION programme in the UK
pathway.unlocks: sensitivity to tiny gravitational and inertial signals in a new frequency band.

pathway.milestone: first experiments looking for entanglement created by gravity alone between two quantum masses
pathway.unlocks: a direct test of whether gravity itself is a quantum field — the sharpest practical question in the field.

pathway.milestone: space-based interferometers such as LISA, planned for the 2030s, plus quantum equivalence-principle tests in free fall
pathway.unlocks: very long baselines free of seismic noise.

pathway.milestone: kilometre-scale or space-deployed quantum sensors comparing clocks, atoms and masses
pathway.unlocks: either a measured deviation from general relativity or the tightest limits yet on quantum gravity.
